findings.title: Least-privilege access
findings.requirement: Limit credentials to named operations and resources, including tenant boundaries. Identify the acting agent separately from the original user or system whose authority it uses. Explicitly authorized, narrowly scoped user delegation is valid; copying a login session or inheriting a person's full permissions is not. Test that an allowed read works and an out-of-scope write, an admin action, and another tenant's data all fail. Limit each access token to its intended audience, so other services reject it. Remove wildcard grants.

findings.title: Credential lifetime and handling
findings.requirement: Issue short-lived credentials from a trusted issuer or managed identity service. For API calls, use expiring access tokens with a specific destination audience, identifying the agent and any explicitly delegated user or system authority, rather than static API keys or personal access tokens. A secrets vault stores backing secrets; it does not itself make a static key into an expiring access token. Keep long-lived secrets out of prompts, images, and checked-in config. Where supported, bind tokens to their holder (mTLS, DPoP, or workload proof tokens). Don't use fixed API keys when short-lived or federated credentials are available. If only static keys are supported, isolate them at the enforcement layer, limit their permissions, and record the lifetime and revocation gap. Show expiry and rotation, including allowed overlap, and explain the chosen lifetime.

findings.title: Destructive-action interception
findings.requirement: List the high-impact operations. These include deletes, destructive database updates, force-pushes, tearing down infrastructure, payment changes, and sending anything outside. Block them by default in the execution path. Allow one only when a reviewer or system with higher authority approves that specific action. When the action runs, authorize its operation, target, and arguments, and block it if they aren't allowed. A list of blocked words or command names is not enough. Test other tools and raw API or shell paths that could do the same thing. Treat deleting audit records, or changing how long they are kept, as high-impact too. That includes asking a more powerful tool or peer to do it. Some agents can do all three of these in one context: read untrusted input, reach sensitive data or systems, and change things or talk to the outside. For those agents, treat every consequential action as high-impact. The exception is a design that stops untrusted content from picking the tool, destination, or arguments. Examples are plan-then-execute, a two-model pattern, or capability tracking such as CaMeL. Record which of the three each agent type has.

Approvals that can be replayed, reused in parallel, or used after expiry
Outside effects left unreconciled after the agent is stopped
A chain of individually allowed actions that adds up to data theft
Tool output not labelled or kept apart from trusted instructions

findings.title: Minimal, isolated runtime
findings.requirement: Remove shells, downloaders, package managers, mounts, and privileges the agent doesn't need. As a container baseline, meet the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards "restricted" profile or the same controls elsewhere. That means non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, and a seccomp profile set. Where supported, also use a read-only root filesystem and user namespaces; the restricted profile doesn't require those two. For running untrusted code, use a sandbox that fits the threat, such as a microVM or a user-space kernel. Ordinary containers share the host's kernel. For managed runtimes, record the provider's isolation evidence and what you can't see. Test that host access is blocked. A blocked probe does not prove the sandbox resists every escape.

That includes API responses (errors and streamed content too), tool and connector output, incoming webhooks and callbacks, messages from other agents, user input, fetched pages, files, and retrieved chunks. findings.title: Complete release manifest
findings.requirement: Write a release manifest: a list of everything that makes up this release. Include the container, harness, system prompt, rules files, model, built-in tools, MCP servers, permission scopes, memory and retrieval settings, identity bindings, network rules, and execution budgets. Include security-policy versions, MCP protocol and extension versions, approved tool-publication config, issuer/audience bindings, and cache/task isolation settings. Add a separate model record for every model: the main agent model, sub-agent models, and helper models such as embedding models and rerankers. For each, record the provider, model ID, exact version or checkpoint, and any adapter or fine-tune version. For training or fine-tuning you run yourself, also record the training job ID, base-model version, training code and config version, dataset version, and the digest of the output. The agent app's release number alone is not enough. Use the [model provenance fields](CHECKLIST-VERIFICATION.md#model-provenance-fields) to separate recorded versions from details a provider doesn't share. Check each model ID you request against the provider's versioning docs. Mark it as a pinned snapshot or as an alias that can change, and record which doc you used and its date. Naming rules differ by provider and model generation. Name each artifact's owner and a reference that can't change, where one exists. A machine-readable format, such as CycloneDX ML-BOM or the SPDX 3.0 AI and Dataset profiles, lets tools check the manifest.

findings.title: Vet and pin dependencies
findings.requirement: Before approving a tool or server, review its source code or available provenance, publisher, permissions, update path, and known vulnerabilities. Include model files, adapters, and datasets. Pin versions or digests, and verify signatures where they exist. A registry's namespace check shows who controls a publisher account, not that the code is safe. Record the limits of remote services and unsigned artifacts, and the extra checks you use instead.

not_covered.problem: A tool's description or schema changing after it was approved
Hidden instructions inside a tool's metadata
Lookalike or duplicate tool names across servers
Container image not pinned by digest or signature-checked

evidence.note: No pip-audit, osv-scanner, trivy or grype step anywhere in the workflow or Dockerfile; the pinned list is never scanned and nothing gates release on vulnerabilities.

checks.check: Each tool, MCP server, package, model file, adapter, and dataset is pinned by exact version or digest, with no floating tags, ranges, or 'latest'.
checks.verify: 1) Open lockfiles, `*.mcp.json`, Dockerfiles, and model or dataset download code. 2) Check each tool, MCP server, package, model file, adapter, and dataset uses an exact version or digest. 3) Answer no if any uses a range, `latest`, a branch, `npx` or `uvx` without a version, or an unpinned download URL.
checks.note: Packages are hash-pinned, base images and Actions are digest/SHA pinned, model is a snapshot. Remote MCP servers (config/tools.yaml:4-13) carry no version or digest, and their implementation is not visible here. CI also uses unpinned yq/jq/pytest from the runner.

checks.check: Signature checks run in the build or load path where the publisher provides signatures, and a failed check stops the install or load.
checks.verify: 1) Find install and load steps in CI and code. 2) Check signature checks (`cosign verify`, `npm audit signatures`, sigstore, GPG) run where the publisher signs. 3) Answer no if a check is missing, its failure is ignored (`|| true`, `continue-on-error`, `try/except` that continues), or a second install path skips it.

findings.title: Re-check tools on load
findings.requirement: Keep a tool publication lifecycle: discovery, review, approval, enablement, re-check, quarantine, and rollback. New servers and tools start disabled; their owner approves descriptions, schemas, permissions, and implementation references before use. Take a fingerprint of each approved tool's description and schema. Compare it whenever the tool loads, its cache refreshes, or its tool list changes. Block unexpected changes until reviewed, including when re-checking fails; don't serve a cached definition as a fallback. Record the policy/config version used at execution, bound propagation delay, and test rollback without restoring revoked access. A metadata hash cannot detect hidden changes to remote code. Pin or attest implementations where visible, record remote visibility limits and review dates, and track affected deployments when vulnerabilities are reported.

not_covered.problem: Hidden instructions in a tool's metadata when first approved
Tool approved without reviewing its publisher and permissions
A new server quietly swapping its tool in for an approved one
Cached tool list shared across authorization contexts

evidence.note: MCP tools start disabled (gateway.py:47) and have stored fingerprints, with config under CODEOWNERS. But the approved record has no implementation reference (version, digest or attestation) for any server and no approval record per version.

checks.check: New tools start disabled, an owner approves versioned definitions and grants before enablement, and approved descriptions/schemas have stored fingerprints.
checks.verify: 1) Trace discovery, approval and enablement on startup and dynamic registration. 2) Check the owner-approved version includes permissions and implementation references and has a stored description/schema hash. 3) Reject auto-enable on discovery, self-approval from untrusted metadata, or fingerprints covering only names. 4) Use unknown for approval service behavior not visible in this repo.
checks.note: MCP tools start disabled (gateway.py:47) and have stored fingerprints, with config under CODEOWNERS. But the approved record has no implementation reference (version, digest or attestation) for any server and no approval record per version.

checks.check: The fingerprint is re-checked on every tool load, cache refresh, and list-changed notice from the server.
checks.verify: 1) List every path that loads tool definitions: startup, cache refresh, reconnect, and the `notifications/tools/list_changed` handler. 2) Check each recomputes the fingerprint and compares it with the stored one. 3) Answer no if any path skips the compare, or both sides of the compare are computed from the new definition.
checks.note: Fingerprints are re-checked only at startup and every 300s. The gateway rejects every method except tools/call (gateway.py:154), so notifications/tools/list_changed is never handled. A changed tool stays enabled up to 300s; the per-call path checks only the _disabled set.

checks.check: When the re-check fails, the tool is blocked and the cached definition is not used.
checks.verify: 1) Open the fingerprint mismatch branch. 2) Check it blocks the tool and does not fall back to the cached definition. 3) Answer no if it only logs, uses the cached or new definition anyway, or an error during the check lets the tool load.
checks.note: A mismatch disables the tool in the gateway (gateway.py:73), but escalate_to_human has a direct_route. Any gateway 503, including the handler's policy_unavailable on an internal error (gateway.py:198), makes the client call the MCP server directly (gateway_client.py:59), skipping the fingerprint/disabled check.

checks.check: The implementation version is pinned or attested where it can be seen, and recorded separately from the metadata fingerprint.
checks.verify: 1) Check how each tool server implementation is referenced: package version, image digest, or attestation. 2) Check that version is recorded in its own field, apart from the metadata fingerprint. 3) Answer no if a visible implementation is unpinned, or only the metadata hash is recorded.
checks.note: Only the metadata fingerprint is recorded; no field records server implementation version, digest or attestation. The servers are owned by other teams, so whether an implementation reference is visible is not known from this repo.

checks.check: Tool quarantine, bounded config propagation, recorded execution config versions, and rollback preserve revocations.
checks.verify: 1) Trace control-plane config to all executors, caches and reload paths. 2) Check a propagation bound and version in execution records. 3) Verify quarantine blocks calls and rollback cannot resurrect revoked grants. 4) Answer no for stale permissions surviving the bound or unsafe rollback; use unknown for runtime guarantees lacking evidence.
checks.quote: return await self._post(spec.direct_route["endpoint"], token, spec, args, ctx, operation_id)
checks.note: Quarantine (the _disabled set, in gateway memory) is bypassed by the direct route. Policy version is recorded in audit rows, but the repo shows no propagation bound or rollback guard that keeps revoked grants revoked.

red_flags_found: src/gateway_client.py:52 Gateway 503 (including its fail-closed policy_unavailable) sends escalate_to_human straight to the MCP server, skipping the fingerprint block.
violates: Compare it whenever the tool loads, its cache refreshes, or its tool list changes
Block unexpected changes until reviewed, including when re-checking fails
findings.summary: Fingerprints are re-checked only every 300s, list_changed is ignored, and a gateway 503 bypasses the block through the direct route.
findings.next_step: Remove direct_route fallback, re-check on list_changed and each load, and record an implementation reference per server.

findings.title: Enforced gateway boundary
findings.requirement: Send MCP calls through a gateway or equivalent enforcement layer the agent cannot bypass. Choose controls for internal HTTP servers, public third-party services, and local stdio servers; private networking and mTLS are one internal deployment pattern, not universal MCP requirements. Authenticate each caller, preserve agent and delegated-subject identity, and authorize each action's tool, operation, resource, tenant, and arguments. Apply the same policy to direct calls, dynamic tools, CLI/code mode, and wrappers. Validate calls and responses, enforce rate limits, and log every decision. For HTTP OAuth, validate access tokens for the gateway's own audience, issuer, expiry, and scopes; obtain separately authorized backend credentials through a trusted issuer or supported exchange. Never accept a token for another resource or relay it unchanged as a substitute for backend authorization. Keep backend secrets and tokens away from agent-controlled execution paths. Restrict local process launch, files, environment, credentials, and network in the host or sandbox. Under MCP 2026-07-28, reject metadata-header/body mismatches before routing or policy relies on them. Isolate private caches by verified authorization context, tenant, resource, and policy version; share only data explicitly approved as public. Authorize explicit task/state handles on every operation; neither a connection nor self-reported metadata establishes identity. Where the gateway is an OAuth client, validate authorization-server issuer responses and protect discovery URLs against SSRF. Record protocol and extension versions and test each enabled extension's boundary, including task access/cancellation and MCP Apps sandbox, CSP, bridge messages, and UI-initiated tool authorization. Test bypass, cross-tenant access, malformed traffic, and required-check outages. Required checks fail closed.

Destructive actions running without a higher-authority approval

findings.title: Protect shared evidence
findings.requirement: Set rules for how long audit records are kept, who can see them, what is redacted, how their integrity is checked, and how they are exported and restored. Test pulling up a past run, and test that missing records or a broken pipeline get noticed. Keep records long enough for investigations and for the law. For example, the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of high-risk systems to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (Articles 19 and 26). High-impact actions must fail closed when required audit capture isn't working.

Secrets left in tool output, responses, or normal logs
